criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community potable water service access for urban poor communities in Metro Manila (specifically Taguig), covering mother-meter sub-connections via community-based Peoples' Organizations (POs), small-scale water providers (SSWPs), and direct individual connections with Manila Water.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines post-privatization water regulatory governance, clientelism, and collective regulatory mobilization. Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly analyzes formal and informal rule-type mechanisms governing service access: privatization concession exclusivity and third-party licensing rules (Certificate of Public Convenience), easing of land-title documentary requirements and connection fees under Manila Water's Tubig Para Sa Barangay (TPSB) program, bulk and retail tariff rules, local legislative enforcement (Taguig Resolution 172 mandating direct connections), conversion of POs into legal cooperatives, and payment accommodation/disconnection discretion.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal empirical case study based on nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork and interviews with local community organizers in Taguig, Metro Manila. Per protocol rules, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with identifiable fieldwork methods are eligible for the systematic review and mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to household/community water connections, service availability, affordability/tariffs (Php 30-35 per unit via POs vs Php 10-12 for direct Manila Water connection), avoidance of service cut-offs via flexible payment arrangements, and expansion of connections (e.g., ~125 member households / ~2,000 residents in Community Water; ~80 POs and ~5,000 households served by remaining POs in Taguig; transition to direct utility connections in 2006).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (urban poor communities/households, ~80 community-based water POs in Taguig including Sitio Imelda in Barangay Upper Bicutan, and regulatory/utility institutions in Metro Manila), the legal/regulatory exposures, the water access/connection and tariff outcomes, and the qualitative ethnographic case study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: Based on almost two years of ethnographic ﬁeldwork in the city of Taguig in Metro Manila, the study shows how community organizations for bringing water to the people acted as the contractors of the private utility.
Normal documentary requirements (especially land titles) were eased and costly connection fees were reduced.
By 2008, Community Water had around 125 member households, serving almost 2,000 individual residents in Sitio Imelda.
Community Water exercised much latitude in allowing members a range of payment means without resorting to cut-offs.
They were accused of charging exorbitant tariffs of Php 30–35 compared with Php 10–12 for a direct connection with Manila Water.
IPD also helped the POs and water cooperatives to engage with the MWSS-RO directly on issues like bulk tariffs, exclusivity, reticulation standards, and compensation for assets.

raw_response.exposure: Post-privatization water concession regulatory structure and access rules in Metro Manila: concession exclusivity and third-party licensing rules (CPC), easing of land-title documentation and connection fees under TPSB, bulk/retail tariff rules, municipal legislative enforcement (Taguig Resolution 172), PO payment accommodation/non-disconnection discretion, and regulatory mobilization by POs and NGOs.
raw_response.outcome: Household and community piped water connections/service access (mother-meter PO sub-connections vs direct individual utility connections), retail tariff/affordability differentials (Php 30-35 vs Php 10-12), and protection against service cut-offs.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban poor residents, households, and community-based Peoples' Organizations (POs) providing water in Taguig, Metro Manila (specifically Sitio Imelda, Barangay Upper Bicutan: 12 POs in Sitio Imelda including Community Water serving ~125 households / ~2,000 residents; ~80 POs across Taguig with remaining POs serving ~5,000 households). Units of analysis: community water organizations (POs), regulatory/utility institutions, and urban poor households/communities.
raw_response.rationale: This socio-legal empirical study based on nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork and interviews in Taguig, Metro Manila examines how post-privatization regulatory rules and community/NGO 'regulatory mobilization' shaped household and community piped water access for the urban poor. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, directly analyzing concession exclusivity clauses, third-party licensing, easing of land-title documentary requirements and connection fees under the TPSB program, bulk and retail tariff disputes, local council enforcement resolutions, and flexible payment accommodation preventing cut-offs.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative ethnographic socio-legal case study (nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork and interviews)
